title: PBOC Work Conference for the Second Half of 2026
locator: PBOC statement republished by the Shanghai municipal financial authorities, paragraphs on monetary policy and financial services. Meeting held 1 August.
summary:
The central bank’s work conference reported ongoing use of moderately loose monetary policy and described operating priorities for the second half. It listed reverse repos, medium-term lending and government bond operations as tools for supplying liquidity at different tenors. It described the introduction of an overnight reverse repo and a narrower band for temporary overnight operations as refinements to short-end control. The statement reported 7.4% year-on-year growth in outstanding social financing and 8.0% in broad money at the end of June. With targeted tools, the aim was to support demand, innovation and smaller firms while continuing to contain financial risks.

The readout describes how the bank intends to implement the stance. In research terms, quantity of liquidity, level of the operative rate and its distribution to borrowers are distinct. The document also notes more flexible cross-border funding arrangements and an overseas official-sector repo facility. Those facilities relate to access to RMB liquidity. The summary of the conference does not identify any realised repricing or a new economy-wide rate decision.

questions.question: Did the narrower overnight band reduce day-to-day variability in traded funding rates?
questions.evidence: Compare DR001 dispersion and operations around matched month-ends, tax dates and settlement days.

questions.question: How much of the additional funding reached smaller or private businesses?
questions.evidence: Compare eligibility and use of the relending tools with new loan flows, spreads and borrower composition.

questions.question: Are overseas official institutions actively using the repo facility?
questions.evidence: Check official uptake and RMB liquidity indicators onshore and offshore.

title: China Monetary Policy Report, Q2 2026
locator: PBOC executive summary. Report released on 12 August according to the PBOC-affiliated Financial News; Suzhou government mirror posted 13 August.
summary:
The PBOC’s second-quarter report describes maintaining a moderately loose stance under a more uncertain external backdrop. It cites 4.7% year-on-year GDP growth in the first half. It pairs ample system liquidity and reduced financing costs with targeted tools for innovation, smaller firms and other preferred sectors. It describes adding overnight reverse repos and narrowing the temporary repo and reverse-repo band from 70 to 50 basis points. It also reports a cut of 25 basis points to the rate on structural monetary tools. That is a change in facility pricing, while the narrower operating band concerns short-end implementation.

The bank reports a first-half average DR001 of 1.31%, a June new corporate loan rate near 3.0%, and a new mortgage rate near 3.1%. It reports the corporate rate about 20 basis points below its prior-year level, while the mortgage rate was broadly flat. Those outcomes suggest looking separately at financing terms by borrower class when assessing transmission. The outlook keeps operations and fiscal coordination flexible and supports orderly moves in the managed RMB float. The summary supplies no market pricing around publication.

questions.question: Does structural relending change financing costs for otherwise comparable firms?
questions.evidence: Match loan originations by borrower risk, location and sector with receipt of programme funding.

questions.question: How do the sources of lower short-end volatility differ at tax dates and ordinary days?
questions.evidence: Compare official operations, government cash flows and DR001 under the wider and narrower operating bands.

questions.question: Does the gap between corporate and mortgage-rate movements indicate different policy transmission?
questions.evidence: Compare changes in loan pricing, margins and borrower or property mix across the two markets.

coverageLimitation: Analysis uses the official executive summary. The full report’s charts and appendices were not independently verified.

title: Monetary Policy Committee Q3 Meeting Readout
locator: Committee readout on 19 September meeting, issued by PBOC on 24 September and republished by the Shanghai municipal authorities on 28 September. Policy stance, operating framework and market stability paragraphs.
summary:
The Monetary Policy Committee called for continued moderately loose policy, stronger countercyclical adjustment and coordination with fiscal policy. Its diagnosis combines a generally stable economy with stronger supply than demand and uneven sector outcomes. It encourages using broad and targeted tools to maintain liquidity, support demand and help prices recover. It says credit-market practices and loan fees should support low all-in financing costs. The readout is a statement of policy direction and gives no new operating rate or fixed timetable.

The committee also says it will watch long yields from a macroprudential perspective and wants markets to determine the exchange rate while guarding against self-reinforcing moves. That supports separate analysis of credit easing, bond-market risks and exchange rate management. The release's reference to earlier low financing costs describes the committee’s assessment at the time, with no data on the market reaction to publication.

questions.question: Which sectors explain the gap between capacity and demand?
questions.evidence: Compare sales, inventories and utilisation by industry, and look at whether financing is associated with changes in those gaps.

questions.question: How do fiscal and monetary actions interact at the short end?
questions.evidence: Match issuer and Treasury cash flows with tenders, repo rates and liquidity around major settlements.

questions.question: Which part of the bond curve reflects term premia rather than near-term rate expectations?
questions.evidence: Compare maturity-specific CGB yields, swaps, issuance and balance-sheet constraints before interpreting changes in the long end.

title: PBOC Adjusts Targeted Monetary Policy Tools
locator: Original PBOC announcement on an official Guangdong mirror, four numbered changes. Associated facilities notices dated 28 September.
summary:
The PBOC lowered its one-year pledged supplementary lending rate from 1.75% to 1.50% and extended eligibility to infrastructure networks including power, water, computing and logistics. The technology and equipment relending quota rose from ¥1.2 trillion to ¥1.4 trillion and the supported proportion increased from 60% to 100%. The combined quota for agriculture, small business and rediscounting went from ¥4.35 trillion to ¥4.85 trillion, of which ¥300 billion was an increase in the private-enterprise quota.

The combination reduces funding costs for one tool and increases the capacity and coverage of other tools. These are prices and limits of particular facilities, while the notice does not measure utilisation or state a new general policy rate. The stated mechanism is to encourage intermediaries to extend credit to eligible projects and borrowers. The strength of that channel depends on banks’ willingness to lend and firms’ investment responses.

questions.question: Do facility drawdowns rise following higher ceilings and support ratios?
questions.evidence: Compare reported drawings, applicant approvals and bank funding use with the revised limits.

questions.question: Which projects gain new credit or lower effective loan costs?
questions.evidence: Compare funded projects, maturities and loan margins before and after revised infrastructure eligibility.

questions.question: Is subsidised funding replacing other loans or supporting additional capital expenditure?
questions.evidence: Match financing records and borrower investments using comparable firms that did not receive support.

title: Ryozo Himino in Saitama: Japan’s Economy and Monetary Policy
locator: Sections I–II, four macro drivers, the discussion of real borrowing rates and charts 6–7.
summary:
Himino described four forces shaping Japan’s outlook. Higher oil costs put pressure on output and pushed prices up. AI-related demand supported output and prices, while currency weakness raised import costs with mixed effects on activity. Financial conditions remained supportive. He said the economy looked resilient in the Tankan, firms’ profits and business investment plans, even though confidence among households was weaker than actual spending. He interpreted wages and scarce labour as supports for consumption.

The speech explains why the 1% nominal policy rate can coexist with accommodation. With rising wages and prices, some borrowers can bear higher nominal payments than in deflation, while depositors may face erosion of purchasing power. Himino pointed to negative short and medium real rates, bank lending appetite and accelerating loan balances. His approach to future adjustments weighs the balance of these channels against the policy outlook. The outcomes he describes precede the speech.

questions.question: How much of the move in import costs was due to exchange rates versus commodity prices?
questions.evidence: Compare import prices in yen and foreign-currency terms and track energy subsidies and firms’ input costs.

questions.question: Is the nominal rate level a good gauge of household cash-flow pressure?
questions.evidence: Compare wage growth, deposit interest and variable-rate mortgage payments across age and leverage groups.

questions.question: Is the AI-led investment impulse visible outside large exporters?
questions.evidence: Check orders, Tankan investment plans and profits by firm size and industry.

coverageLimitation: The official HTML transcript and its chart references were reviewed. The separate figure pack was not independently checked.

title: Change in the Guideline for Money Market Operations
locator: Decision §§1–3, implementation footnotes and named dissent.
summary:
Japan’s Policy Board voted 7–2 to set its uncollateralised overnight call-rate guideline at around 1.25%. The new rate became effective 24 September. The deposit facility moved to 1.25% and the basic loan rate to 1.50% on the same date. The Board also voted unanimously to set a floating rate and a quantity limit for funding to support private sector climate efforts. The operational adjustments apply to different types of central-bank funding and should be tracked separately.

The statement relates the increase to the central bank’s assessment of underlying inflation approaching the 2% target and financing conditions remaining accommodative. The two dissenters favoured the previous setting, with reservations about current inflation and strength of activity. That difference makes the subsequent policy path conditional even after a second hike of the year. The document identifies the policy change, vote and effective date. A repricing analysis would require announcement-time rather than implementation-time prices.

questions.question: Did short rates move mainly on the decision or on subsequent guidance?
questions.evidence: Compare yen overnight swaps at separately verified release times for the decision and press conference.

questions.question: How closely did traded call rates track the new guideline after implementation?
questions.evidence: Compare traded overnight rates, facility use and passage to term funding before and after 24 September.

questions.question: Which data could bring the dissenters closer to the majority?
questions.evidence: Compare subsequent speaker views and meeting votes with incoming consumption and measures of underlying inflation.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan)
title: Foreign Exchange Reserves as of the End of July 2026
locator: Release’s reserve total, three drivers and portfolio exposure note.
summary:
The CBC reported reserves of US$594.27 billion at end-July, US$2.88 billion below the previous month. It attributed changes to investment returns, valuation changes in non-dollar reserve currencies and interventions to smooth volatile capital flows. It separately reported holdings of securities and Taiwan dollar deposits by foreign portfolio investors of US$1,663.1 billion. That stock can inform exposure work. It is a different measure from actual portfolio outflows.

Reserve valuation, investment income and trading can offset one another. The net decline therefore does not identify the direction or size of all official foreign exchange transactions. The report concerns the balance at the end of July, which is distinct from the report date of 5 August.

questions.question: How much of the change in reserves was transactional after allowing for valuation?
questions.evidence: Compare published net FX purchases and sales alongside currency movements and reserve income estimates.

questions.question: Which flows were most associated with currency volatility?
questions.evidence: Separate net foreign equity turnover, realised outward remittance and forward hedge adjustments.

questions.question: How liquid were FX markets when the bank intervened?
questions.evidence: Review spot and forward liquidity indicators, trading volumes and the timing of unusually large flows.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan)
title: Financial Conditions (July 2026)
locator: Official bulletin, monetary aggregates and loans and investments paragraphs.
summary:
The CBC reports July declines in daily-average M1B and M2 of 0.71% and 0.09% from June. Growth from a year earlier nonetheless measured 7.34% and 7.42%, respectively, with net foreign capital outflows contributing to slower annual growth. The measure of loans and investments rose 9.07% from a year earlier, primarily because of claims on government and public enterprises. The broader adjusted financial institutions measure, including life insurer activity and certain reclassified loans, rose 7.40%.

The release gives reasons for measuring both funding and asset composition and distinguishing monthly changes from year-over-year comparisons. Lower deposits and larger public-sector claims can coexist. The release covers July balances and is not an announcement of a new rate or liquidity operation.

questions.question: Did outflows affect specific types of deposit funding disproportionately?
questions.evidence: Compare FX and domestic deposit components with portfolio flow and currency settlement data.

questions.question: How much of claims growth reflects public rather than private financing?
questions.evidence: Compare the report’s sector breakdown with issuance and loan origination measures.

questions.question: How sensitive are the reported rates to definition changes or valuation?
questions.evidence: Check total and adjusted series and differences between cost-basis and reported market exposures.

coverageLimitation: The analysis uses the official HTML bulletin. The linked workbook was not independently reviewed.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan)
title: Monetary Policy Decision of the Board Meeting (2026 Q3)
locator: Sections II–V: forecast, policy-rate hold, selective credit controls, and FX framework.
summary:
The CBC kept its discount rate at 2.00%, secured refinancing at 2.375%, and temporary accommodations at 4.25%. It saw contained inflation despite a substantial upward adjustment to its growth outlook. Technology exports and investment supported an 11.48% growth forecast for 2026, with the Bank projecting 5.82% for 2027 against a high base. Core and headline forecasts remained just above 2% for 2026 and were expected to ease below 2% in 2027. Its assessment of the external energy shock and inflation outlook supported a hold while monitoring global conditions, capital flows and domestic prices.

The board separately eased a targeted constraint: the second-home mortgage loan-to-value ceiling rose from 60% to 70%, and a construction-timing affidavit for land loans was removed. The changes took effect 18 September. The CBC linked the adjustment to a decline in banks’ real estate lending concentration and improvements in internal controls. The mortgage decision could affect particular borrowers independently of the policy rate. The statement also retained scope for FX intervention during disorderly conditions.

questions.question: How much does the growth forecast depend on a few AI-related industries?
questions.evidence: Compare exports, output, investment and household demand by industry using the same release vintage.

questions.question: Does loosening second-home LTV ceilings alter financing availability?
questions.evidence: Check new mortgage LTV, approval rates, pricing and credit concentration around implementation.

questions.question: What would unsettle the below-2% inflation forecasts for 2027?
questions.evidence: Compare the assumed oil path, energy relief and service-price persistence with incoming component data.

coverageLimitation: The full statement was reviewed. The separately linked comparative forecast tables and regulatory appendix were not independently checked.

title: Monetary Policy Decision and Opening Remarks
locator: Decision and opening remarks, especially growth, inflation, financial stability and dissent paragraphs.
summary:
The Monetary Policy Board raised the Base Rate by 25 basis points to 3.00%. Strong exports and recovering domestic demand meant growth had exceeded expectations. The Bank expected inflation to remain above target for a considerable time. The Board cited the risk that persistent price pressure would broaden and pointed to financial stability concerns as reasons to act. It described a semiconductor upswing and investment as supports to output. Higher energy prices were one source of inflation that could still pass through to other prices.

The decision statement separates market developments before the meeting from the future policy direction. Government yields had been affected by global fiscal risks as well as policy expectations. The Board said additional hikes would depend on the course of inflation and activity and risks in property and household debt. One member preferred a hold. This is the documented decision and reasoning as of 27 August, without a measurement of the surprise relative to the priced path.

questions.question: What was priced before the 25 basis-point move?
questions.evidence: Compare timestamped Korean rates around the decision and opening remarks with prior expected meeting rates.

questions.question: Was inflation pressure spreading into demand-sensitive prices?
questions.evidence: Check oil and FX pass-through, services inflation and household price expectations.

questions.question: Would stronger demand and housing credit point to similar policy risks?
questions.evidence: Track private consumption and Seoul-region transactions alongside mortgage and total household flows.

title: Monetary Policy Report (September 2026)
locator: Official Korean original. Overview and Parts I–II on operating conditions, decisions and forward guidance.
summary:
The Bank of Korea’s September report reviews two consecutive increases in July and August that raised the Base Rate from 2.50% to 3.00%. It places the moves in the context of stronger exports and investment, recovering consumption, above-target inflation and financial stability risks around property and household loans. It says timing and pace of further increases depend on the evolution of those factors. The earlier spring holds allowed a read of developments in the Middle East before the policy rate was adjusted.

Its discussion of financial markets separates global government bond spillovers and local rate expectations from corporate credit spreads and refinancing. It sees pronounced differences in access to finance among some issuers even when market-wide pricing appears stable. This distinction matters when assessing tightening through credit conditions. This is the September assessment, when it was published in Korean. The full English edition was published separately in November.

questions.question: Did the export upswing feed through to broader domestic wages and spending?
questions.evidence: Compare industry hiring and output with consumption and real income through the same report vintage.

questions.question: How much of the rise in long yields reflected global rates as opposed to domestic policy expectations?
questions.evidence: Compare Korean swaps and government yields with overseas benchmark spreads and issuance patterns.

questions.question: Are refinancing constraints concentrated in particular credit segments?
questions.evidence: Review corporate spreads and realised refinancing by rating and collateral, with separate attention to short-term project finance.

coverageLimitation: The Korean text and published explanations were reviewed. The linked source workbook and underlying data for every exhibit were not independently verified.

title: Minutes of the Monetary Policy Board Meeting (August 2026)
locator: Official publication abstract, 27 August policy meeting majority decision and named dissent.
summary:
The official minutes release records the majority’s preference to raise the Base Rate from 2.75% to 3.00% for the interval before the next meeting. Kunil Hwang preferred keeping the rate at 2.75%. The release attributes the majority’s decision to the combined domestic and global economic and financial circumstances. The publication date of 15 September is distinct from the 27 August decision date.

The vote by itself identifies a disagreement about current timing. The abstract does not provide the member-by-member reasoning or say how the dissenting member would respond to different inflation or housing outcomes. Any attempt to track future preference should use the full stated arguments and subsequent votes.

questions.question: Which arguments differ between the vote summary and full minutes?
questions.evidence: Compare the attached member contributions with the decision statement and the policy press conference.

questions.question: Does the identified dissent reflect a different outlook or a different preference for waiting?
questions.evidence: Read the individual argument against later statements and incoming data known as of each meeting.

questions.question: Was the content newly available on 15 September important for prices?
questions.evidence: Compare the release with disclosures already public on 27 August and measure the announcement-time move separately.

coverageLimitation: The official English abstract was readable. The individual discussion in the linked PDF was not verified.

title: Loan Prime Rates for 20 August 2026
locator: PBOC-authorised National Interbank Funding Center statement, two published lending benchmarks and effective period.
summary: The authorised announcement put the one-year loan prime rate at 3.00% and the five-year-plus rate at 3.50%, with both valid until the next fixing. The quoted tenors are distinct references for lending rather than realised borrowing rates or a complete funding curve. The fixing identifies the published references; assessing how a bank passes them through calls for separating contract pricing and changes in bank margins, credit risk and borrower composition. The brief source gives no forecasts, decision rationale or release-window repricing.

questions.question: Did effective rates change for new short- and long-tenor borrowing?
questions.evidence: Compare bank loan originations by tenor, collateral and borrower segment with the corresponding published benchmark.

questions.question: How far do the benchmarks transmit into stock rather than only new loans?
questions.evidence: Track floating reset dates, fixed shares and refinancing costs across vintages.

questions.question: Where would any release surprise appear first?
questions.evidence: Compare expectations known before the fixing with subsequent movements in onshore swaps and loan rates on separately timed releases.

title: Notice on Overnight Reverse Repos Around the End of September
locator: Open-market business notice no. 9 of 2026, dated 23 September and posted on the official Heilongjiang mirror on 24 September.
summary:
The PBOC announced that it would conduct overnight reverse repos from 28 September to 8 October to match banks’ short-term liquidity needs. These operations were set up as quantity tenders at a fixed rate and subject to a daily maximum of ¥1 trillion. The notice specifies the operating period and ceiling but gives neither a transaction amount nor a new rate level. The timing makes it relevant to how overnight funding needs change across the quarter-end and adjoining dates.

A tender adds available liquidity at the tenor offered. On a net basis the effect also depends on maturities and other operations. The announcement does not establish whether later traded repo rates moved because of the schedule. Daily tender results and funding quotes would help distinguish the availability of support from actual take-up and realised rates.

questions.question: Did the scheduled operations offset an unusual short-term funding demand?
questions.evidence: Compare calendar-matched repo rates, turnover and dispersion around quarter-end using official operation dates.

questions.question: How far below the headline ceiling did actual usage fall?
questions.evidence: Compare daily allocations and maturities, incorporating other injections and drains.

questions.question: Did funding relief extend beyond deposit-taking institutions?
questions.evidence: Compare DR001 with broader repo rates and volumes over the same dates.

title: Outlook for Economic Activity and Prices (July 2026, full text)
locator: Bank’s View and Box 2 on AI demand. Full report released 3 August, following the Bank’s View at the July meeting.
summary:
The July Outlook projected moderate growth in fiscal 2026 at a slower pace than before, because expensive oil weighed on activity while fiscal measures, domestic financing conditions and global AI demand offered support. Growth forecasts were little changed from the previous round and expected to improve from fiscal 2027 as the oil drag faded. The Board expected CPI excluding fresh food to accelerate to well above 2% from the second half of fiscal 2026, then ease toward 2%. Compared with the previous forecast, government measures helped lower the fiscal 2026 CPI forecast.

The report distinguishes that measured CPI profile from underlying inflation, which it expected to approach the 2% objective as wages, pricing behaviour and expectations became more supportive. It judged growth risks generally balanced and warned about upside price risks. Its separate discussion of AI demand matters because the effects can support activity and lift input prices together. The document records the July baseline and policy assessment made public in full in August.

questions.question: How sensitive is the inflation baseline to government mitigation of energy costs?
questions.evidence: Compare forecast assumptions with an unsubsidised energy price scenario and check the CPI component weights.

questions.question: What part of the growth path depends on AI exports and equipment demand?
questions.evidence: Use the report's AI box, trade quantities and sector order data to test concentrations and spillovers.

questions.question: Which measures would confirm inflation near target after temporary costs fade?
questions.evidence: Compare trend inflation, wages and expectations, keeping institutional price changes separate.

coverageLimitation: Analysis draws on the Bank's View and selected sections. Full chart and box verification is incomplete.

title: Summary of Opinions at the July 30–31 Monetary Policy Meeting
locator: Policy summary §§I–II, emphasis on transmission lags and conditions for adjustments. An edited account of July opinions.
summary:
Opinions published after the July meeting indicate differing views on timing. One assessment supported holding while testing whether June's hike would affect domestic activity and inflation with a lag of about one to one and a half years. Other comments found that negative short real rates, favourable bank lending and underlying inflation approaching 2% still made the direction of further hikes appropriate. A more forceful view pointed to upside price risks and the possibility of a faster pace than markets expected if conditions called for it.

Participants considered the drag of higher crude oil and the support of technology-related demand. Wages, pricing behaviour and longer-term expectations mattered for whether inflation would remain near target. The Bank’s document is an edited set of remarks rather than a count of preferences by stance. It gives no new voted decision on the August publication date.

questions.question: Where would earlier hikes first appear in bank-intermediated credit?
questions.evidence: Compare new loan rates, quantities and term changes in mortgage and firm borrowing.

questions.question: What could bring forward the next adjustment?
questions.evidence: Compare sector-level price pressure and wage data with evolving guidance and separately observe the market-implied schedule.

questions.question: Can the relative weight of inflation and lag concerns be inferred by member?
questions.evidence: Consult subsequent named speeches and vote records in addition to this unattributed document.

title: Hajime Takata in Sapporo: Economic Activity, Prices, and Monetary Policy in Japan
locator: Sections I–II, July proposal, post-bubble stages, and the discussion of flexible rate adjustments.
summary:
Takata explained why at the July meeting he had proposed raising the rate to 1.25% after June’s move to 1%. He saw 2026 as a new phase for Japan. His account traces the shift from deflation and subdued investment through unconventional easing to companies investing and borrowing more readily. He judged those changes to be evidence that the Bank was close to achieving price stability. Improving global technology demand and the turn toward higher foreign policy rates made him prefer flexibility on timing instead of relying on the earlier cadence.

His reading implies that higher oil prices and a changing global rate environment should be assessed through their impact on Japanese inflation and financial conditions. The speech sets out his own rationale and proposal at the previous meeting. It gives neither an agreed Board path nor a measured market surprise.

questions.question: Are corporate pricing and wage behaviours persistently different from the deflationary period?
questions.evidence: Compare compensation, output prices and investment at firm level across different shocks and size groups.

questions.question: What foreign rates or currency channels could warrant a faster adjustment?
questions.evidence: Compare trade-weighted yen and interest differentials with domestic import and wholesale price pass-through.

questions.question: How much of the action Takata advocates is already priced?
questions.evidence: Compare pre-speech near-dated yen rates and implied volatility with separately timed moves after publication.

coverageLimitation: The transcript and its chart references were reviewed. The separate figures file was not independently audited.

title: Kazuyuki Masu in Fukui: Economic Activity, Prices, and Monetary Policy in Japan
locator: Price risk sections, the interpretation of charts 7–8 on real and neutral rates, and policy conduct.
summary:
Masu argued that negative short real rates deserved early attention in an economy that had left deflation. At the time the 1% policy setting was below the lower end of his illustrative 1.1–2.5% nominal neutral range. He built that range by adding the 2% objective to a broad set of model estimates of the natural real rate. He cautioned that neutral could not be pinned to a single number. Persistently negative short real rates could support leverage, encourage businesses to bring investment forward and reduce the purchasing power of households’ savings.

Different shocks implied different policy trade-offs. The Middle East shock affected output as well as input prices; a weaker yen amplified imported prices but was not itself the policy target. AI demand offered an offset for activity and raised some prices. Food inflation could persist beyond rice or energy because of distribution and packaging costs. The evidence and rate assessment represent Masu’s views as expressed in September.

questions.question: How sensitive is the rate gap to estimated expectations and methods?
questions.evidence: Compare several measures of expected inflation and trend growth when constructing a range of real and neutral rates.

questions.question: Is rising food inflation spreading after removing narrowly volatile items?
questions.evidence: Track processed-food prices, distribution and packaging costs and selling-price revisions.

questions.question: How exposed is Japan if global investment in AI equipment decelerates?
questions.evidence: Compare semiconductor materials and equipment exports, orders and corresponding profit sensitivity.

coverageLimitation: The official transcript was reviewed. The standalone chart pack was not independently validated.

title: Minutes of the July 30–31 Monetary Policy Meeting
locator: Sections II–III and policy vote records near the end; release 28 September for the July meeting.
summary:
The minutes record an 8–1 July vote to maintain the overnight guideline around 1%. Takata proposed 1.25% because he believed underlying inflation had reached the target and saw value in getting closer to neutral faster. Other members backed leaving the guideline at its earlier level. Approval of the statement text and approval of the Outlook’s Bank’s View are different decisions, with their own results. The release makes visible the difference between the policy rate vote, the personal proposal and the text voted on.

The meeting considered simultaneous pressures from expensive energy and a more robust technology cycle. Staff reports also describe ongoing reductions in Japanese government bond purchases under the June plan. These are historical minutes published in September after the later decision. Their July description of rates should not be read as a fresh September setting.

questions.question: Which details add information beyond the August summary of opinions?
questions.evidence: Compare the policy-vote details and draft proposals with the earlier condensed version and statement.

questions.question: How do differences in the outlook relate to the hold vote?
questions.evidence: Compare the separate outlook and operating-guideline votes and subsequent public rationales by named members.

questions.question: How did the purchase schedule affect the long end?
questions.evidence: Combine actual JGB operations and issuance with maturity-specific term premia and liquidity indicators.

coverageLimitation: The voting record and key policy discussion were checked. Detailed staff exhibits and every subsection were not independently verified.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan)
title: Interbank Call Loan and Commercial Paper Markets (July 2026)
locator: Sections I–II, overnight rates and turnover, primary and secondary paper observations.
summary:
In July the weighted overnight call-loan rate averaged 0.824%, up 0.001 percentage points, while interbank turnover and average daily balances rose. Longer private funding showed a different pattern. For commercial paper of one to thirty days, the preliminary primary average fell 8 basis points to 1.87% while the secondary average rose 14 basis points to 1.68%. The figures describe aggregates in markets with different issuer, maturity and transaction mixes, so the difference cannot by itself measure a bank or issuer premium.

The same publication shows a decrease in the amount of commercial paper outstanding even as overall short-term bills rose. That distinction matters if using turnover or outstanding amounts to diagnose funding pressure. The release reports July outcomes on 7 August and announces no change of monetary-policy setting.

questions.question: Does the divergence in commercial paper survive a maturity and issuer match?
questions.evidence: Compare matched primary and secondary observations by rating and remaining tenor.

questions.question: Did larger interbank turnover reflect broader conditions or calendar effects?
questions.evidence: Compare daily data on rates, turnover and borrower mix at similar month-ends.

questions.question: Which securities explain the increase in bills outstanding?
questions.evidence: Use the issuance table and change in component stocks to separate commercial paper from other bills.

coverageLimitation: The official release text was checked. The separate detailed table file was not independently reviewed.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan)
title: Foreign Exchange Reserves as of the End of August 2026
locator: Reserve level and change, valuation/management/transaction factors, foreign portfolio investor exposure note.
summary:
The CBC reported reserves of US$601.90 billion at the end of August, an increase of US$7.63 billion from July. It lists reserve investment returns, changes in the US dollar value of other reserve currencies and central bank operations to smooth volatile flows. The higher reserve total does not quantify any single contribution. Foreign portfolio investors held securities and Taiwan dollar deposits valued at US$1,861.0 billion, reported as 309% of reserves. That is an exposure comparison. It does not specify the timing or size of possible future flows.

For an FX review, this release records the monthly reserve outcome and describes intervention as one channel. It does not say how the market reacted when the public received the figure on 4 September.

questions.question: Which part of the increase was due to reserve valuation?
questions.evidence: Combine observable exchange-rate changes and available reserve allocation disclosures with net official transactions.

questions.question: Was the higher foreign portfolio value driven by new investment or asset revaluation?
questions.evidence: Compare net buying, deposits and equity price changes in local currency and US dollars.

questions.question: How does the bank's intervention signal compare with observable currency moves?
questions.evidence: Review dated spot and forward trading data alongside later official purchase or sales totals.

institution: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan)
title: Financial Conditions (August 2026)
locator: Monetary aggregates and loans and investments paragraphs; August observations published 23 September.
summary:
The August financial conditions release reports that M1B and M2 grew from July on a daily-average basis, by 0.72% and 0.65%. Their annual rates declined to 6.65% and 6.79%, respectively. The CBC links the slower growth in broad money mainly to slower growth in foreign-currency and passbook savings deposits. Loans and investments of monetary financial institutions grew 9.43% from a year earlier, compared with the revised prior rate of 9.08%, with stronger growth in claims on private borrowers and government enterprises. Including insurance company lending and adjustments for reclassification and write-offs gives a lower annual growth rate of 7.69%.

The divergence between deposit growth and asset growth suggests checking composition and financing separately. These data do not themselves establish whether lending standards loosened or demand accelerated.

questions.question: Which deposits drove the change in broad money growth?
questions.evidence: Examine the component tables with consistent assumptions on exchange rates and deposit definitions.

questions.question: Does the higher growth of claims reflect new credit or changes in stock treatment?

title: Economic Outlook (August 2026)
locator: Official forecast release, real GDP outlook, headline and core prices, cost and demand drivers.
summary:
The August forecast put real growth at 3.3% for 2026 and 2.9% for 2027. Its rationale is that the semiconductor upswing continued and positive effects were reaching a broader set of activities despite uncertainty surrounding the Middle East. Headline CPI was projected at 2.7% and 2.3%, while core inflation was forecast at 2.5% in each year. The Bank linked the underlying pressure to pass-through of earlier cost shocks and gradually stronger demand.

The forecast combines stronger activity and elevated core inflation with a lower year-ahead headline forecast. That distinction is relevant for evaluating underlying price pressure if energy effects unwind. The figures are projections available on 27 August, with no market-price observations included in the public summary.

questions.question: What evidence would confirm the widening semiconductor spillovers?
questions.evidence: Compare output, employment and domestic investment beyond the companies and industries driving exports.

questions.question: Does persistent core inflation come from remaining cost pass-through or current domestic demand?
questions.evidence: Decompose core CPI and track wages and firm pricing by industry.

questions.question: How sensitive are the two forecast years to the same energy assumption?
questions.evidence: Compare the forecast's oil and FX assumptions with plausible alternatives and trace effects through CPI.

coverageLimitation: Analysis uses the official forecast summary. The PDF annex and its individual exhibits were not independently checked.

title: Who Moved the Career Ladder? AI and Youth Employment in Korea
locator: Bank of Korea Issue Note 2026-19 publication summary, worker- and industry-level findings and identification caveats.
summary:
The authors use pension subscriber and labour-force survey data to study young workers during the spread of AI. They report that high-exposure industries accounted for 268,000 of a 285,000 fall in youth employment between June 2022 and June 2026. The losses were stronger in industries using AI for automation. Exposure associated with augmentation showed no comparable pattern. They also observe fewer entrants and more exits, meaning a hiring-only explanation misses one margin. Some industries where youth employment declined still added employees in their fifties.

The public research summary explicitly cautions against treating exposure as identification of causation. Reversing pandemic hiring, preferences for experienced workers, changing training and remote work also matter. The proposed focus is supporting pathways into experience and skills as technology changes, rather than mechanically preserving existing posts. This is staff research about structural labour markets.

questions.question: Can the estimated exposure correlate with labour demand changes that predate AI diffusion?
questions.evidence: Test pre-existing trends by sector and occupation and compare actual AI adoption with exposure scores.

questions.question: What explains the split between new entry and exits?
questions.evidence: Compare suitably matched worker transitions and training histories using cohort data.

questions.question: Does use of AI for augmentation help young workers build experience?
questions.evidence: Measure subsequent wages, retention and promotions in firms with different adoption patterns.

coverageLimitation: Analysis covers the public summary. The full issue-note appendix and robustness exhibits were not independently verified.

title: Hyun Song Shin: Opening Address at the BOK–CEPR–OECD Conference
locator: Bank of Korea dated speech page and official BIS republication of the speaker’s remarks. Structural policy agenda and summary of research topics.
summary:
The governor framed ageing as central to productivity, potential growth and the equilibrium interest rate. He presented the issue as a set of long-run channels rather than a single demographic forecast: worker supply, knowledge diffusion, technology adoption and the capacity for fiscal adjustment. Korea’s experience can illuminate these questions for other economies. He highlighted contributions in the conference programme on low fertility, the budget implications of ageing and the extent to which technology might offset a smaller workforce.

The governor described potential gains from AI without treating them as sufficient on their own. The remarks identify research questions relevant to estimates of productive capacity and the neutral rate. The speech gives no new view on the next decision, and the conference studies are proposals or examples he introduces rather than results independently established in this short address.

questions.question: How large are contributions from participation and productivity under plausible ageing paths?
questions.evidence: Build alternative potential growth estimates with cohort-specific labour supply and productivity data.

questions.question: Could technology offset ageing in some sectors before it does so in the aggregate?
questions.evidence: Compare employment, capital intensity and realised output across firms adopting different technologies.

questions.question: How do ageing-related fiscal pressures influence the longer-term neutral rate?
questions.evidence: Compare estimated saving, investment and government financing under matched demographic scenarios.
